content.title: Absolute Value, Radical, Rational, and Exponential Equations
content.overview: This guide covers the methods for solving four common types of nonlinear equations found in SAT Math: absolute value, radical, rational, and exponential equations. The focus is on mastering specific solution techniques for each type and learning to identify invalid solutions by checking the domain.
learning_objectives: Master the case-by-case method for solving absolute value equations
Learn to solve radical equations by squaring both sides and identifying extraneous solutions
Use cross-multiplication or the common denominator method to solve rational equations
Apply the property of equal bases to solve basic exponential equations

sections.title: Absolute Value Equations
sections.content: Absolute value represents the distance of a number from the origin and is therefore always non-negative. When solving an equation of the form |ax + b| = c: 1. If c < 0, the equation has no solution. 2. If c ≥ 0, split it into two linear equations: ax + b = c or ax + b = -c. After solving these, substitute them back into the original equation to verify.

sections.title: Radical Equations
sections.content:
Radical equations typically involve arithmetic square roots. Steps to solve: 1. Isolate the radical term. 2. Square both sides of the equation to eliminate the radical. 3. Solve the resulting equation. Note: The squaring process may introduce "extraneous solutions," which are solutions that satisfy the squared equation but not the original one. You must substitute solutions back into the original radical to ensure the value under the radical is non-negative and the radical result is non-negative.

![Solving Radical Equations Process](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/de2ba878-e46f-4968-bbad-0932802a7f4a-1786502046594-142.webp)

sections.title: Rational Equations
sections.content: Rational equations have variables in the denominator. Main methods: 1. Cross-multiplication (applicable for proportions). 2. Multiplying by the Least Common Denominator (LCD) to eliminate denominators. After solving, you must check if the denominator is zero; any solution that makes a denominator zero is invalid.

sections.title: Exponential Equations
sections.content: In the SAT, basic exponential equations can usually be solved by converting them to the same base. If a^x = a^y where a > 0 and a ≠ 1, then x = y. If the bases are different, try rewriting the bases as powers of the same base (e.g., writing both 4 and 8 as powers of 2).

worked_examples.question: Solve the equation: √(2x + 7) - x = 2
worked_examples.solution: 1. Isolate the radical: √(2x + 7) = x + 2. 2. Square both sides: 2x + 7 = (x + 2)² -> 2x + 7 = x² + 4x + 4. 3. Arrange into a standard quadratic equation: x² + 2x - 3 = 0. 4. Factor: (x + 3)(x - 1) = 0, giving x = -3 or x = 1. 5. Verify: Substitute x = -3, √[2(-3)+7] - (-3) = √1 + 3 = 4 ≠ 2 (discard). Substitute x = 1, √[2(1)+7] - 1 = √9 - 1 = 2 (holds). Therefore, the solution is x = 1.

worked_examples.question: Solve the equation: 3 / (x - 1) = 6 / (x + 2)
worked_examples.solution: 1. Cross-multiply: 3(x + 2) = 6(x - 1). 2. Expand: 3x + 6 = 6x - 6. 3. Move terms: 12 = 3x. 4. Solve: x = 4. 5. Check denominators: When x = 4, x - 1 = 3 and x + 2 = 6, neither of which is zero. Therefore, the solution is x = 4.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to consider the negative case when solving |x| = k (i.e., only solving x = k and ignoring x = -k).
Failing to substitute solutions back into the original equation after squaring both sides of a radical equation, leading to the inclusion of extraneous solutions.
Ignoring the restriction that denominators cannot be zero after solving a rational equation.
Incorrectly assuming that exponents can be set equal even if the bases are different in an exponential equation.
exam_tips: If an equation looks difficult to solve, try substituting the values from the answer choices into the original equation (back-solving).
When you see a radical equation, your first thought should be 'I must check for extraneous solutions in the final step.'
For rational equations, quickly observe the denominators to eliminate options that would make any denominator 0.
content.recap: The key to solving nonlinear equations lies in 'reduction' or 'linearization,' but these processes (such as squaring or clearing denominators) often change the domain of the original equation. Therefore, verifying the validity of solutions is the final line of defense to ensure you get the points.

knowledge_claims.content: When solving the absolute value equation |ax + b| = c, if c is positive, you must solve ax + b = c and ax + b = -c separately.
If an absolute value expression is equal to a negative number (e.g., |x + 5| = -2), the equation has no solution in the set of real numbers.
The first step in solving a radical equation is usually to isolate the radical term so that it stands alone on one side of the equals sign.
Squaring both sides of a radical equation may produce extraneous solutions, so all obtained solutions must be verified by substituting them into the original equation.
An extraneous solution is a value produced during the equation transformation process that satisfies the transformed equation but does not satisfy the original equation.
When solving a rational equation, denominators can be eliminated by multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common multiple of all denominators.
Solutions to a rational equation must satisfy the condition that the denominator is not zero; if a solution makes any denominator zero, it must be discarded.
For the exponential equation a^f(x) = a^g(x), if the base a is a constant greater than 0 and not equal to 1, then it can be concluded that f(x) = g(x).
If the bases of an exponential equation are different (e.g., 2^x = 8), one should attempt to unify the bases (e.g., writing 8 as 2^3) before comparing the exponents.
In a radical equation, the result of an arithmetic square root (√x) is defined as a non-negative number.
